record.paper_title: NTN-based 6G Localization: Vision, Role of LEOs, and Open Problems
record.context_brief: GNSS-free NTN access through standalone RAT-dependent localization
record.original_question: How can user equipment (UE) that lacks Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) capability estimate its location well enough to close a radio link and connect to a non-terrestrial network (NTN), using standalone radio-access-technology-dependent cellular positioning methods rather than UE-reported GNSS?

evidence.quote: To close a radio link with a satellite, a UE must calculate the relative speed and RTT of the service link, for timing and Doppler resolution.

Hence, GNSS capability is mandatory for NTN access, and UEs without GNSS are out of the scope of 5G NTN. As we will discuss further, this sets the stage for a new set of design problems where UEs without GNSS can be localized using standalone RAT-dependent methods and hence can connect to NTN.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a user equipment (UE) on or near the Earth's surface that wishes to establish a radio link with a low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellite belonging to a non-terrestrial cellular network. To successfully close such a link, the UE must compensate for (i) the round-trip propagation delay between itself and the satellite and (ii) the Doppler frequency shift induced by the satellite's high relative velocity; both compensations require knowledge of the UE's approximate geographic position. In current cellular standards this position is supplied by an onboard Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) receiver, but assume that the UE has no GNSS capability and that no other UE-side absolute positioning source is available.

The satellite (or the network) is assumed to know its own ephemeris (position and velocity at every time instant) and can transmit downlink reference signals with known waveforms, timing, and carrier frequency. The UE can measure features of received downlink signals (e.g., received power, time of arrival relative to its local clock, carrier-frequency offset, angle of arrival if it has multiple antennas) from one or more satellites that may pass over it, possibly at different times.

Design and rigorously analyze a standalone radio-access-technology–dependent positioning scheme — i.e., a scheme that uses only such cellular downlink/uplink measurements between the UE and satellites, with no GNSS or other external positioning input — that produces an estimate of the UE position with accuracy sufficient to enable initial timing advance and Doppler pre-compensation, and hence radio-link closure with the non-terrestrial network. In particular:

1. Identify the minimal set of measurements (number of satellites, number of time epochs, types of signal observables) needed for the UE position to be observable, given satellite ephemeris and an unknown UE clock bias and frequency offset.
2. Derive the Cramér–Rao lower bound (or an equivalent fundamental accuracy limit) on UE position estimation as a function of carrier frequency, bandwidth, signal-to-noise ratio, satellite geometry, and the number of observation epochs.
3. Determine the maximum positioning error tolerable for successful initial access (link closure) as a function of the orbital and waveform parameters, and specify regimes in which the proposed scheme meets this tolerance.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem of GNSS-free initial-access localization for UEs connecting to LEO-based non-terrestrial networks is an active open research area. 3GPP Release 17/18 NTN specifications still require UEs to report GNSS-derived position for initial access, and recent research papers (2023–2025) on LEO-based positioning, Doppler/delay-based UE localization, and 6G NTN initial access continue to propose partial solutions (e.g., Doppler-only, multi-satellite TDOA/FDOA schemes) but do not provide a fully standardized, validated standalone RAT-dependent positioning method that closes the radio link for GNSS-less UEs.
